title: Fed Delivers First Rate Hike Since 2023 as Sticky Inflation Meets a Stronger Economy
excerpt: The Federal Reserve lifted its benchmark rate to 3.75%–4.00% in a unanimous vote, arguing a resilient economy gives it room to attack inflation it now says won't reach 2% until 2029.
body:
• The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark rate by a quarter point to 3.75%–4.00% on September 16, the first U.S. rate hike since July 2023, in a unanimous 12–0 vote.
  • Chair Kevin Warsh argued a resilient economy gives the Fed room to attack inflation it calls too high for too long: "the plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long."
  • Officials now project PCE inflation at 3.7% for 2026 and do not expect 2% until 2029; 16 of 18 policymakers see at least one more hike before year-end.
  • Economists say the move reflects a structural shift: the 15-year era of low rates and low inflation is giving way to a higher-priced, higher-rate world.

The Federal Reserve on Wednesday raised its benchmark interest rate for the first time in more than three years, declaring that sticky inflation and a surprisingly durable economy demand a tougher stance on prices. The unanimous vote to lift the federal funds target range by a quarter percentage point, to 3.75%–4.00%, ended a stretch of five consecutive holds this year.

The range had sat at 3.50%–3.75% since the December 2025 cut. In its September statement, the FOMC said economic activity is "expanding at a solid pace," job gains have kept pace with workforce growth, and unemployment has changed little, holding near 4.1%. The verdict on prices was blunt: "Inflation remains elevated."

A decision long in the making

The unanimity was the real message. Minutes from the July meeting showed three officials already favored a hike; by September, concern about renewed price pressure had spread across the full committee.

Chair Kevin Warsh, who took the helm in May, said the action would support "a timelier return to the committee's 2% goal," describing it as removing "a dose of accommodation" from a strong economy. He also defended the Fed's independence, a signal the tightening path is not up for negotiation.

"The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long."

— Kevin Warsh, Federal Reserve Chair

The projections alongside the decision painted a sobering picture. Officials now see PCE inflation at 3.7% for 2026, up from 3.6% in June, and the median expectation for a return to 2% has slipped to 2029. Growth forecasts edged up to 2.3% this year and 2.4% next. And the dot plot signaled this may not be a one-off: 16 of 18 policymakers expect at least one more increase before year-end, with one meeting left on the 2026 calendar.

What’s driving the pressure

The inflation impulse this time is one the Fed did not create. Brent crude has traded above $108 a barrel — roughly 50% higher than when the Iran war began in late February — after tanker attacks and Iran's near-closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The average U.S. pump price reached $4.32 a gallon, and record diesel costs have raised transport costs across groceries and furniture. Consumer prices rose 3.4% in August from a year earlier. The labor market has not cracked: employers added 162,000 workers in August.

President Donald Trump criticized the decision shortly after it was announced, renewing his call for lower rates and alleging — without evidence — that policymakers raised rates for political reasons. He said he continued to have confidence in Warsh but disagreed with the decision.

A regime change, not a cycle

Economists argue the hike reflects something larger than a rate decision. Big tech firms are borrowing heavily to fund data-center construction while the federal government keeps running large deficits — trends that point to higher rates regardless of what the Fed does. As the Associated Press reported, the low interest-rate, low-inflation world that lasted nearly 15 years after the Great Recession is over; the average 30-year mortgage rate reached 6.95% last week, the highest in more than a year and a half.

"We've undergone a structural transformation of the economy," said Joe Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM. "The regime change in inflation and interest rates is the outcome." Healthy consumer and business spending, he noted, is now colliding with supply shocks and bottlenecks — from energy prices to chip and labor shortages hampering the AI buildout.

"We've undergone a structural transformation of the economy. The regime change in inflation and interest rates is the outcome."

— Joe Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM

What to watch

The Fed has one more decision this year, and the dot plot suggests it is more likely to tighten again than to sit still. The new range remains well below the 5.25%–5.50% reached in 2023 — but the direction of travel, and the era it reflects, has changed.
